description: Emma Bovary confuses real life with the sentimental novels she has read. Flaubert invented the modern novel and the trial that made it famous.

hero.hook: A woman who is bored in the provinces. Then adultery, debts, and a word that will become a diagnosis.

blocks.text: In **1857**, **Gustave Flaubert** published **Madame Bovary**, a novel about a woman disappointed by the province and sinking into adultery. The book marks a break in literature.  was born here: this movement wants to describe life as it is, without idealizing it. **[[realism]]**

Flaubert will be tried for immorality. His trial will make the novel a scandal, then a classic. Through **Emma Bovary**, he questions the power of fiction on our lives. The book shows how dreams fueled by reading can destroy reality.

**Gustave Flaubert** isolated himself in **Croisset**, near Rouen, and devoted **five years**, from 1851 to 1856, to this novel. His rule: the “right word”, the exact word, neither too much nor too little, without repetition or lyrical emphasis. The writer must become invisible: it is the style that counts, not the author who puts himself forward.

blocks.caption: Flaubert: the craftsman of pure style.

blocks.text: “Madame Bovary, it’s me”: Flaubert is not talking about autobiography, but about total immersion in the pain of his heroine.

He hates shoddy **romanticism**, hollow romanticism full of clichés, while recognizing in it the temptation of dreams. This tension fuels Emma's drama. Flaubert also wrote famous letters where he recounted his nights of work in each sentence.

sections.title: Flaubert and the asceticism of the right word

blocks.text: **Emma Rouault** grew up in the convent with sentimental novels, stories full of exalted passions. She marries **Charles Bovary**, an honest but dull country doctor. The couple settles in **Yonville-l'Abbaye**, a small Norman town where nothing resembles the heroines Emma has read.

blocks.caption: The Normandy province: setting for the boredom that pushes Emma towards adultery.

blocks.text: To escape boredom, Emma loves **Rodolphe Boulanger**, lord of the region, then **Léon Dupuis**, notary's clerk. Each lover turns out to be as banal as their husband. The merchant **Lheureux** pushes her into debt: her credit purchases ruin her. The novel is inspired by a news item: the affair of **Delphine Delamare**, who died in **1848**.

sections.title: Emma: the clash between dream and reality

blocks.text: Flaubert invents the . This technique mixes the narrator's voice with the character's thoughts, without quotation marks or "she thought that". The reader accesses Emma's thoughts while maintaining an ironic distance. We no longer always know if it is Emma or the narrator who is speaking. **[[free indirect style]]**

In **1857**, Flaubert was acquitted of “insulting public morals”. Emma commits suicide with the **arsenic** stolen from the apothecary , a figure of the triumphant and mediocre bourgeoisie. Charles dies of grief, their daughter **Bertha** goes to work in a factory, and **[[Homais]]** receives the cross of honor. No poetic justice: the world remains unfair.

The philosopher **Jules de Gaultier** coined the term : the chronic dissatisfaction of someone who prefers fantasy to reality. Emma is not just an adulterous woman. She is the first great figure of modern frustration linked to consumption, the desire for objects, luxury and passions. **[[Bovarysm]]**

Flaubert elevates the form above the subject: a book about “nothing”, the life of a bored woman, can be a masterpiece if the style is perfect. Each scene is constructed like a painting, with precise details that reveal Emma's inner emptiness. **Marcel Proust**, **Franz Kafka** and the **New Novel**, a 20th century movement that breaks narrative conventions, owe a lot to him. The trial of 1857 also transformed the novel into a subject of public debate.
**Madame Bovary**, published in **1857**, revolutionizes the novel with  and : confusing real life with the fiction we read can lead to disaster. **[[free indirect style]]** **[[Bovarysm]]**
